title: Churches around the world
hookLine: from Ethiopian round churches to Korean hilltop crosses

lines: A ROUND CHURCH IN A RING OF TREES.
RED CROSSES ACROSS A NIGHT CITY.
cards: On a green Ethiopian hillside, a church stands in a ring of old trees. Its walls make a circle, its roof rises to a point, and people in white shawls stand outside the doors and pray toward the center.
Now cross the world to a Korean city after dark. From a high window, red crosses glow on rooftops all over the hills, like a field of small lit signs. Same faith, two very different buildings.
Neither looks like the white steeple some people picture when they hear the word church.

teach.h: TO THE UTTERMOST PART OF THE EARTH.
teach.b: Start with a promise in Acts. Before Jesus is taken up, he tells his friends: "ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth."
A few chapters later, the story leaves the map. An official from Ethiopia, riding home in his chariot and reading the prophet Isaiah, meets Philip on a desert road.
They pass water, and the man says: "See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?" Next, the round church.

teach.h: A ROUND CHURCH, THE HOLY PLACE AT ITS HEART.
teach.b: In the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, some churches are built in a circle, rings within rings, with the most holy place at the very center, where only priests go.
The building is a map of drawing near to God: outer ring, inner ring, heart. In Lalibela, tradition says, churches were carved straight down into solid rock.
Then the lit crosses. In Korea, crosses glowing red or white at night mark churches across the cities. A church there might be a single floor above a shop.
The shape is new; the prayer inside is the same old prayer. Last, a conversation at a well. A Samaritan woman asks Jesus which mountain is the right place to worship.
He answers: "the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father." No one mountain, no one shape.
A church in the rock, in a ring of trees or above a shop can bear the same name.

how: Christians around the world worship in buildings of many shapes: round churches and rock-hewn churches in Ethiopia, domed churches in the Orthodox world, Gothic cathedrals, white wooden chapels, and churches above shops in Korean cities marked by lit crosses.

the many shapes one faith's buildings take worldwide

o: the hour is coming for neither one.

practice: Find a photo of a church far from where you live, a round church in Ethiopia, a wooden church in the far north, a church in a Korean city, and look slowly: the doors, where the light comes in, what's at the center.
Then imagine the people who'll walk in this week, and what they'll carry with them. If you pray, you can pray for that congregation; if you don't, simply hold them in mind for a moment.

wordCard.voice: Churches around the world. Round, carved, domed, lit up at night: the many shapes the same faith takes in different places.

orig.note: Greek: assembly. the New Testament's word for church names people, as in "the church that is in their house."

carryVoice: Your line: many shapes. One faith, built in many places. See you tomorrow.
